question: Where does the fact that a dispatcher is running live — a detached process with a file saying so, a terminal you leave open, or the dashboard server that already runs?

options.label: A foreground `sober dispatch` you leave running, Ctrl-C stops it
options.reason: This is the shape the repository already has: `sober dashboard` is described in the help as "serve the board in a browser — Ctrl-C stops it and its runs", so a second long-lived command is a pattern the user has already met. Liveness is the process itself — nothing on disk to go stale, nothing to reap, and a crash is visible in the window where it happened. It composes with whatever the user already uses to keep a process alive.
options.costLater: It occupies a terminal, and closing the laptop lid or the window ends it silently — the user believes work is draining and it is not. There is no way to ask "is one running" from another shell without looking for the process, so the twice-started case has to be caught through the writer lock rather than a straight answer.

options.label: A detached process with a pidfile under .sober/local
options.reason: It survives the terminal, which is the whole point of unattended dispatch — approve a chain, close the window, come back to reviews. `.sober/local/` already exists and is already disposable by design, so a pidfile there is in a directory that expects exactly this kind of thing, and `start`/`stop`/`status` become answerable questions from any shell.
options.costLater: A pidfile is a second copy of a truth the operating system already holds, and it goes stale in every way files do — killed process, reused pid, a machine that slept. That is a staleness rule to write, test and explain, on top of the one ADR 0025 already has for the writer lock. Detached also means its output goes to a log nobody is watching, so a dispatcher failing in a loop is silent until someone looks.

options.label: A loop inside the dashboard server, which is already a long-lived process
options.reason: SOBER already has exactly one long-lived process and ADR 0008 gave the dashboard a server; adding the drain loop there means no new process, no new lifecycle, and no second thing to start. The watch surface is then free — the queue view is a page on a server that is already serving the board.
options.costLater: It ties dispatching to having a browser-facing server running, which is the one part of SOBER a headless or remote user does not want. It also puts spending money on agents inside the process whose job was to display things, so anyone stopping the dashboard to free a port stops the queue without meaning to.
